cards.question: What is Birrell's paper "An Introduction to Programming with Threads" (1989)?
cards.answer: A tutorial (from DEC SRC) on using threads correctly: fork/join, mutexes, condition variables, and alerts.
cards.memory: The programming model behind pthreads and the course's threads lectures.
distractors: A redesign of the SunOS kernel around kernel threads.
A user-level threads library that runs many threads on a few LWPs.
A study of web server architectures for disk-bound workloads.

cards.question: Birrell's threads paper gives five reasons to use threads. What are they?
cards.answer: Use multiprocessors, overlap work with slow devices, keep a user interface responsive, serve many network clients at once, and defer work to cut latency.
distractors: Save memory, avoid locks, avoid scheduling, improve portability, and improve security.
Avoid system calls, avoid interrupts, avoid I/O, avoid caches, and avoid IPC.
Replace processes, replace the kernel, replace signals, replace pipes, and replace files.

cards.question: In Birrell's thread API, what does Fork(proc, arg) do, and what does it return?
cards.answer: Starts a new thread running proc(arg) and returns a handle to that thread.
distractors: Runs proc(arg) in the caller's thread and returns its result.
Creates a new process running proc(arg) and returns its process ID.
Queues proc(arg) to run later and returns nothing.

cards.question: In Birrell's thread API, what does Join(handle) do?
cards.answer: Waits for that forked thread to finish, then returns the result of its procedure.
distractors: Merges two threads into one.
Starts the thread named by the handle.
Waits until the thread reaches a mutex, then returns.

cards.question: Birrell observes that Join is rarely called in real programs. Why?
cards.answer: Most forked threads are long-lived daemons (or report results another way), so no one waits for them to finish.
distractors: Join is too slow to use in practice.
Join can deadlock, so programmers avoid it.
Threads are joined automatically when they hold no mutex.

cards.question: In Birrell's thread API, what does the LOCK m DO … END clause do?
cards.answer: Acquires mutex m, runs the enclosed statements, then releases m automatically.
cards.memory: Holding m is the only way to touch the data m protects, like a monitor.
distractors: Acquires m and keeps it until the thread exits.
Runs the statements only if m is free, otherwise skips them.
Disables interrupts while the statements run.

cards.question: In Birrell's thread API, what does Wait(m, c) do?
cards.answer: Atomically releases mutex m and blocks on condition variable c; when woken, it re-acquires m before returning.
distractors: Blocks on c while keeping m locked.
Releases m, then checks c once without blocking.
Signals c, then blocks until m is free.

cards.question: Why must a condition variable's Wait(m, c) release the mutex and start blocking as one atomic step?
cards.answer: Otherwise a Signal sent in the gap between releasing m and blocking would be missed, and the thread could sleep forever.
distractors: So the mutex can never be held by two threads at once.
So Broadcast wakes threads in FIFO order.
So the waiting thread keeps its scheduling priority.

cards.question: In Birrell's thread API, how many waiting threads does Signal(c) wake?
cards.answer: At least one, and possibly more (Broadcast(c) wakes all of them).
cards.memory: Because Signal may wake more than one thread, every waiter must re-check its condition.
distractors: Exactly one, always.
None until the signaler releases the mutex.
Only the thread that has waited the longest.

cards.question: Birrell says to always write WHILE NOT condition DO Wait(m, c) END rather than using an IF. Why?
cards.answer: Another thread may grab the mutex and change the state first, and Signal may wake more than one thread, so the condition must be re-checked after every wake-up.
cards.memory: It also lets you check correctness by looking at the waiting code alone.
distractors: WHILE is faster than IF for condition checks.
Wait only works inside a loop.
IF would release the mutex twice.

cards.question: What is an alert in Birrell's thread API?
cards.answer: A request, sent to a specific thread, asking it to abandon a long wait or computation.
distractors: A kernel notification that a device finished I/O.
A warning that a deadlock was detected.
A condition variable that wakes every waiter.

cards.question: In Birrell's thread API, which call lets a thread blocked on a condition variable be woken by an alert, and what happens when it is?
cards.answer: AlertWait (used instead of Wait): if the thread is alerted, AlertWait raises the Alerted exception.
distractors: TestAlert: it returns true when the thread is alerted.
Wait: it returns early and clears the alert.
Join: it passes the alert on to the parent thread.

cards.question: In Birrell's thread API, how does a thread that is busy computing (not waiting) find out it has been alerted?
cards.answer: It calls TestAlert, which polls whether an alert is pending.
distractors: It calls AlertWait, which blocks until an alert arrives.
The kernel interrupts it with a signal.
It can't; alerts only affect waiting threads.

cards.question: Birrell says a mutex protects an invariant. What is that invariant?
cards.answer: A property of the shared data that holds whenever the mutex is unlocked (it may be broken only while the mutex is held).
distractors: A variable that never changes once it is set.
The rule that only one thread runs at a time.
The order in which threads acquire the mutex.

cards.question: Birrell: Wait(m, c) releases mutex m while the thread sleeps. What must the thread do before calling Wait?
cards.answer: Restore m's invariant, because other threads will see the shared data as soon as m is released.
distractors: Release m itself.
Signal every other condition variable.
Nothing; Wait saves the shared data for it.

cards.question: Birrell's race example: two threads both run table[i] := r; i := i + 1 with no mutex. What can go wrong?
cards.answer: Both store into the same table[i] before either increments i: one entry is lost and a slot is left empty.
distractors: Deadlock: both threads wait for each other forever.
Nothing; each statement is atomic.
The program crashes with an out-of-bounds error.

cards.question: What rule does Birrell give for avoiding deadlock when threads need several mutexes?
cards.answer: Impose a partial order on the mutexes and always acquire them in that order.
distractors: Give each mutex its own condition variable.
Always use Broadcast instead of Signal.
Never hold a mutex for more than one statement.

cards.question: Locking granularity: what do you gain and lose by splitting one coarse lock into many fine-grained locks?
cards.answer: Gain: more concurrency (fewer threads conflicting on the same lock). Lose: simplicity (more complex code).
cards.memory: Birrell's example: one lock for the whole open-file table plus one lock per open file.
distractors: Gain: simpler code. Lose: concurrency.
Gain: less memory. Lose: correctness.
Gain: nothing; fine-grained locks only add overhead.

cards.question: What is priority inversion? (Birrell's example: high-priority A, medium-priority B, low-priority C, and mutex M.)
cards.answer: C holds M and A blocks waiting for M, but B keeps the CPU, so C never runs to release M and A is stuck behind B.
distractors: A runs forever and starves B and C.
A and C each hold a mutex the other needs.
The scheduler runs C before A because C has waited longer.

cards.question: What is the standard fix for priority inversion?
cards.answer: Priority inheritance: a thread holding a mutex temporarily runs at the priority of the highest-priority thread waiting for it.
cards.memory: Birrell described the problem, but SRC didn't implement a fix. Eykholt's SunOS kernel did, using turnstiles.
distractors: Lock ordering.
Adaptive mutexes that spin instead of blocking.
Using Broadcast instead of Signal.

cards.question: Birrell on double-checked initialization: a thread reads a shared variable without holding its mutex, to avoid locking. When is that unlocked read acceptable?
cards.answer: Only when the value is treated as a hint (confirmed under the lock), and only if the language guarantees the read is safe.
distractors: Always, because reads never change data.
Whenever the variable is a single integer.
Never, under any circumstances.

cards.question: Birrell's readers/writer lock: with one condition variable shared by readers and writers, a Broadcast wakes threads that still can't proceed. What does Birrell call this problem?
cards.answer: Spurious wake-ups.
cards.memory: Terminology trap: the P2L2 lecture uses "spurious wake-up" for what Birrell calls a spurious lock conflict.
distractors: Spurious lock conflicts.
Priority inversion.
The nested monitor problem.

cards.question: How does Birrell fix spurious wake-ups in his readers/writer lock?
cards.answer: Use separate condition variables for readers and writers, so a wake-up only reaches threads that can proceed.
distractors: Signal only after releasing the mutex.
Count the waiting writers.
Replace Broadcast with a spin loop.

cards.question: Birrell: on a multiprocessor, a thread woken by Signal immediately blocks again, because the signaling thread still holds the mutex. What does Birrell call this?
cards.answer: A spurious lock conflict.
cards.memory: The P2L2 lecture calls this a spurious wake-up.
distractors: A spurious wake-up.
Priority inversion.
A deadlock.

cards.question: How does Birrell avoid spurious lock conflicts?
cards.answer: Signal after leaving the LOCK clause (after releasing the mutex), so the woken thread can take the mutex right away.
distractors: Use separate condition variables for readers and writers.
Hold the mutex across both the Signal and the Wait.
Use Broadcast instead of Signal.

cards.question: In Birrell's readers/writer lock, a steady stream of readers can keep a writer waiting forever. How does he fix this?
cards.answer: Count waiting writers, and make new readers wait whenever a writer is waiting.
distractors: Give writers their own mutex.
Limit the lock to one reader at a time.
Broadcast to writers before readers.

cards.question: Birrell's readers/writer lock grew from 15 to 30 lines after his fixes for spurious wake-ups, lock conflicts, and starvation. What advice does he draw from that?
cards.answer: Every fix adds complexity, so add one only if the actual load needs it.
distractors: Always add every fix up front.
Never use readers/writer locks; use a plain mutex.
Move the lock into the kernel to keep the code short.

cards.question: What is Birrell's nested monitor problem?
cards.answer: A thread holding outer mutex a calls Wait inside monitor b. Wait releases only b's mutex, so the thread that would Signal it, which must lock a first, can never get in: deadlock.
distractors: A monitor procedure calling itself recursively.
Two threads waiting on the same condition variable.
A signal handler locking a mutex the interrupted thread holds.

cards.question: Birrell's pipeline example (PaintChar → Rasterize → Painter) runs each stage in its own thread. How do the stages pass work along?
cards.answer: Through producer-consumer queues between the stages.
distractors: Each stage Joins the previous stage's thread.
Through unlocked global variables.
By sending signals between processes.

cards.question: Birrell: in a threaded pipeline, what limits how much concurrency you can get?
cards.answer: The number of stages (at most one thread busy per stage), and only if the stages are balanced.
distractors: The length of the queues between stages.
The number of mutexes in the program.
Nothing; adding threads always adds concurrency.

cards.question: Birrell: which threads hurt performance: runnable threads beyond the number of processors, or threads blocked waiting (e.g., on I/O)?
cards.answer: Extra runnable threads. Blocked threads are cheap.
distractors: Blocked threads; runnable threads are free.
Both cost the same.
Neither; thread count never affects performance.

cards.question: Birrell: why shouldn't you Fork a new thread for a tiny task?
cards.answer: Forking isn't free (roughly the cost of 2–3 scheduling decisions), which can outweigh a tiny task's work.
distractors: Fork copies the whole address space.
Tiny tasks can't acquire a mutex.
The OS limits each process to a few threads.

cards.question: Birrell: when one thread blocks on I/O or a page fault, what must the thread system guarantee?
cards.answer: Only that thread blocks; the process's other threads keep running.
cards.memory: That's what kernel threads provide, and what Flash's MT server depends on.
distractors: Every thread in the process blocks until the I/O finishes.
The blocked thread is killed and restarted.
The OS switches to a different process.

cards.question: Birrell: what is an up-call?
cards.answer: A lower layer calling directly up into a higher layer (e.g., when a network packet arrives), instead of passing the work up through queues, to avoid a context switch per layer.
distractors: A system call from user mode into the kernel.
A thread raising its own priority.
A signal sent from a child process to its parent.

cards.question: Birrell: what locking rule applies when a lower layer makes an up-call into a higher layer?
cards.answer: Don't hold a mutex while making the up-call.
distractors: Hold every mutex for the whole up-call.
Disable interrupts during the up-call.
Only the main thread may make up-calls.

cards.question: Birrell: what are version stamps used for in threaded programs?
cards.answer: Detecting stale cached data: if the stamp has changed, the cached copy is out of date.
distractors: Ordering mutex acquisition.
Numbering threads so they can be joined.
Recording which CPU a thread last ran on.

cards.question: Birrell: what is a work crew?
cards.answer: A fixed pool of threads that take requests from a shared queue.
cards.memory: Birrell's work crews = the lecture's boss-worker pattern; his pipelining = the pipeline pattern.
distractors: A chain of stages with one thread per stage.
One new thread forked per request.
A group of processes sharing memory.

cards.question: Birrell: how should a library's entry points behave so the library works well in threaded programs?
cards.answer: Be thread-safe and synchronous.
distractors: Be asynchronous, with callbacks.
Be callable from only one thread.
Be lock-free and never block.

cards.question: What are the main limitations of Birrell's threads paper as evidence?
cards.answer: It's a tutorial with no experiments, selective and biased toward SRC's own design, with Modula-2+ examples not meant for production.
distractors: Simulation only, with synthetic workloads.
Uniprocessor only, on a small-memory machine.
No end-to-end benchmarks; assumes interrupts rarely block.

cards.question: What did Eykholt et al. do in "Beyond Multiprocessing: Multithreading the SunOS Kernel" (1992)?
cards.answer: Rebuilt the SunOS 5.0 (Solaris 2.0) kernel around kernel threads, making it fully preemptible, real-time capable, and ready for symmetric multiprocessors.
distractors: Added a user-level threads library on top of the unchanged kernel.
Replaced the SunOS kernel with a microkernel.
Added a few locks to the old kernel and nothing else.

cards.question: Eykholt et al.: just adding locks to the old SunOS kernel wasn't enough. What three goals did the multithreaded kernel need to meet?
cards.answer: Concurrency on symmetric multiprocessors, multiple threads per user process, and bounded real-time dispatch latency.
distractors: Portability, security, and a smaller memory footprint.
Faster disk I/O, faster file systems, and faster networking.
User-level scheduling, green threads, and coroutines.

cards.question: In the multithreaded SunOS kernel, what is a kernel thread?
cards.answer: The unit the kernel schedules onto a CPU: just a small data structure plus a stack.
distractors: A full process with its own address space.
A user-level thread the kernel can't see.
A hardware context on a multithreaded core.

cards.question: In SunOS/Solaris, what is an LWP (lightweight process)?
cards.answer: A kernel-supported thread of control inside a user process.
distractors: A kernel thread that belongs to no user process.
A user-level thread the kernel can't see.
A lightweight copy of the parent process made by fork.

cards.question: In SunOS/Solaris, every LWP has a kernel thread. Does every kernel thread have an LWP?
cards.answer: No. Kernel-only threads (e.g., kernel daemons and interrupt threads) have no LWP.
distractors: Yes; the two are always one-to-one.
Yes, but some LWPs have no kernel thread.
No; kernel threads and LWPs are unrelated.

cards.question: The multithreaded SunOS kernel splits execution state across four kinds of data structures. What are they?
cards.answer: Per-process (proc), per-LWP, per-kernel-thread, and per-CPU.
distractors: Per-user, per-group, per-session, and per-terminal.
Per-page, per-segment, per-file, and per-device.
One combined process control block per process.

cards.question: On SPARC, what does register %g7 point to inside the multithreaded SunOS kernel?
cards.answer: The current kernel thread (curthread).
cards.memory: In user space, Stein & Shah's threads library uses %g7 for the current user thread's thread-local storage.
distractors: The current process's page table.
The interrupt vector table.
The current CPU's run queue.

cards.question: What three scheduling classes does the multithreaded SunOS kernel support?
cards.answer: System, timesharing, and real-time.
distractors: Batch, interactive, and idle.
FIFO, round-robin, and lottery.
Kernel, user, and interrupt.

cards.question: The multithreaded SunOS kernel is fully preemptible. When is kernel preemption turned off?
cards.answer: Only inside small, bounded sections of kernel code.
cards.memory: Keeping those sections short is what bounds real-time dispatch latency.
distractors: Whenever any mutex is held.
For the whole of every system call.
Never, not even briefly.

cards.question: SunOS adaptive mutex: a thread finds the mutex already locked. How does it decide whether to spin or sleep?
cards.answer: It spins while the lock's owner is running on another CPU; otherwise it sleeps.
distractors: It always spins for a fixed number of cycles, then sleeps.
It sleeps while the owner is running, and spins otherwise.
It spins only on single-CPU machines.

cards.question: Why does a SunOS adaptive mutex spin only while the lock's owner is running?
cards.answer: A running owner will probably release the lock soon, so spinning beats sleeping. An owner that isn't running won't release it soon, so spinning would just waste the CPU.
distractors: Spinning is only allowed in user mode.
A running owner can't be preempted.
Spinning makes the owner run faster.

cards.question: In the SunOS kernel, which kinds of locks get priority inheritance, and why those?
cards.answer: Mutexes and writer (exclusive) locks, because they have a single owner whose priority can be boosted.
distractors: Reader locks, because they have many owners.
Condition variables, because they have waiting threads.
Spin locks, because they never sleep.

cards.question: In the SunOS kernel, what is a turnstile?
cards.answer: A per-lock structure holding the lock's sleep queue and priority-inheritance information (more predictable than shared, hashed sleep queues).
distractors: A spin lock used only by interrupt handlers.
A per-CPU queue of runnable threads.
A counter that limits how many threads can enter a lock.

cards.question: SunOS handles interrupts as threads. When an interrupt thread takes over a CPU, what happens to the thread it interrupted?
cards.answer: It's pinned: it can't run anywhere else until the interrupt thread finishes or blocks.
distractors: It's moved to another CPU's run queue.
It's destroyed and restarted later.
It keeps running alongside the interrupt thread.

cards.question: SunOS handles interrupts as threads. When does an interrupt handler become a full, independently scheduled thread?
cards.answer: Only if it blocks (e.g., on a mutex). Until then it runs cheaply, borrowing the interrupted thread's CPU.
distractors: On every interrupt.
Only for timer interrupts.
Only when the interrupted thread was idle.

cards.question: SunOS handles most interrupts as threads. What about interrupts above "thread level" (the highest interrupt priorities)?
cards.answer: They are not handled as threads and may use only spin locks, because they must never block.
distractors: They always become full threads.
They may block on any mutex.
They are ignored until the CPU is idle.

cards.question: SunOS pre-allocates threads for interrupt handling. About how much memory does each interrupt thread cost?
cards.answer: About 8 KB.
distractors: About 1.7 KB.
About 1 MB.
About 128 MB.

cards.question: What are the main limitations of Eykholt et al.'s multithreaded SunOS kernel paper?
cards.answer: No end-to-end benchmarks; the net-gain argument for interrupt threads assumes interrupts rarely block; deadlock detection misses reader locks and condition variables.
distractors: No experiments at all; it's a tutorial biased toward one lab's design.
Simulation only, with synthetic workloads.
Uniprocessor only, with simulated WAN conditions.

cards.question: What problem does Stein & Shah's "Implementing Lightweight Threads" (1992) address?
cards.answer: Giving every thread its own LWP wastes kernel resources, because most threads are idle at any moment.
distractors: The SunOS kernel couldn't be preempted.
Web servers block on disk I/O.
Multithreaded cores leave the pipeline idle.

cards.question: Stein & Shah's threads library: how does it map user-level threads onto the kernel?
cards.answer: M:N: it multiplexes many cheap user-level threads onto a small, self-adjusting pool of LWPs.
distractors: 1:1: one LWP per user thread.
M:1: all user threads on a single LWP.
It doesn't; every thread is a separate process.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, what is a bound thread?
cards.answer: A user-level thread permanently attached to its own LWP.
distractors: A thread that shares the LWP pool with other threads.
A thread that can't receive signals.
A thread whose stack size is fixed at creation.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, when would you make a thread bound instead of unbound?
cards.answer: When it needs system-wide scheduling scope, e.g., real-time scheduling.
cards.memory: Unbound threads are cheaper: they share the LWP pool.
distractors: When it only does short computations.
When it never blocks.
When you want it to use less memory.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, what is an unbound thread?
cards.answer: A user-level thread with no LWP of its own; it shares the pool of LWPs with other unbound threads (the default, cheapest kind).
distractors: A thread permanently attached to one LWP.
A thread with no stack.
A thread detached from its creator.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, where does a thread's thread-local storage (TLS) live, and what does it hold?
cards.answer: At the base of the thread's stack; it holds the thread structure and a per-thread errno.
cards.memory: On SPARC, %g7 points to the current thread's TLS.
distractors: In the kernel's LWP structure; it holds the signal mask.
On the heap; it holds the thread's return value.
In a global table; it holds the thread ID.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, what five states can a user-level thread be in?
cards.answer: RUNNABLE, ACTIVE (running on an LWP), SLEEPING, STOPPED, and ZOMBIE.
distractors: New, ready, running, waiting, and terminated.
Bound, unbound, parked, idle, and dead.
Created, joined, detached, alerted, and exited.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, how does the library choose which user-level thread runs next?
cards.answer: From a user-level priority queue with fixed priorities.
distractors: Round-robin, driven by a kernel timer per thread.
By CPI, mixing CPU-bound and memory-bound threads.
The kernel schedules every user thread directly.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, what does an LWP do when there is no runnable thread for it to run? (The paper calls this idling.)
cards.answer: It waits on a global condition variable until a thread becomes runnable.
distractors: It waits on one specific thread's semaphore.
It is destroyed immediately.
It spins until a thread is ready.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, a bound thread blocks. What does its LWP do? (The paper calls this parking.)
cards.answer: It waits on that thread's own semaphore; it can't run any other thread meanwhile.
distractors: It waits on a global condition variable and runs any runnable thread.
It is returned to the LWP pool.
It is destroyed and recreated when the thread wakes.

cards.question: How does Stein & Shah's threads library preempt a user-level thread that is running on an LWP?
cards.answer: It sets a flag on the thread, then sends that LWP a SIGLWP signal.
distractors: It sends SIGWAITING to the process.
It asks the kernel to destroy the LWP.
It waits until the thread calls yield.

cards.question: In Solaris with Stein & Shah's threads library, when does the kernel send a process SIGWAITING?
cards.answer: When every LWP in the process is blocked.
distractors: When a thread waits on a condition variable.
When an LWP has been idle for 5 minutes.
When a mutex has more than one waiter.

cards.question: What does Stein & Shah's threads library do when the process receives SIGWAITING?
cards.answer: Adds an LWP to the pool, so runnable user-level threads can run.
cards.memory: SIGWAITING and Flash's helper processes both fix "one blocking call stalls everything."
distractors: Kills the blocked threads.
Removes an idle LWP from the pool.
Ignores it until a thread yields.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, what does thr_setconcurrency(n) do?
cards.answer: Gives the library a hint about how many LWPs to keep for unbound threads.
distractors: Sets a hard limit on the number of threads.
Binds n threads to their own LWPs.
Sets the scheduling timeslice to n milliseconds.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, what happens to LWPs that stay idle for a long time?
cards.answer: After about 5 minutes idle, they are aged out (destroyed).
distractors: They are kept forever in case they're needed.
They are turned into bound threads.
They trigger SIGWAITING.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, what happens when a detached thread exits?
cards.answer: It goes on deathrow; a reaper thread later frees it and caches its stack for reuse.
distractors: It waits as a zombie until another thread joins it.
Its memory is freed immediately.
It stays until the whole process exits.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, what happens when an undetached thread exits?
cards.answer: It stays a zombie until another thread calls thr_join on it.
distractors: It goes on deathrow for the reaper.
Its memory is freed immediately.
It is restarted from the beginning.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, how is a mutex or condition variable implemented when only one process uses it?
cards.answer: With user-level sleep queues inside the library (no kernel involvement).
distractors: With kernel synchronization on the LWP.
With spin locks only.
With signals between LWPs.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, how is a mutex or condition variable implemented when it lives in memory shared by several processes?
cards.answer: With kernel synchronization on the LWP, identified by the shared memory's file and offset.
distractors: With user-level sleep queues inside the library.
With spin locks only.
It isn't supported.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, how does an LWP's signal mask compare with the mask of the user-level thread it's running?
cards.answer: Equal or less restrictive, so the kernel may deliver a signal that the current thread has masked.
distractors: Always more restrictive.
Always identical.
Unrelated; LWPs have no signal mask.

cards.question: In Stein & Shah's threads library, a signal arrives on an LWP whose current user-level thread has it masked. What happens?
cards.answer: The library's signal handler re-sends it to a thread that has it enabled.
distractors: The signal is dropped.
The masked thread handles it anyway.
The process is terminated.

cards.question: With an M:N threads library like Stein & Shah's, why can't the kernel deliver a signal directly to the right user-level thread?
cards.answer: The kernel can't see user-level threads or their signal masks, because threads change their masks at user level without a system call.
distractors: Signals can only be sent to whole processes.
The kernel can see the masks but ignores them for speed.
User-level threads have no signal masks.

cards.question: What are the main limitations of Stein & Shah's lightweight threads paper?
cards.answer: No performance data at all; SIGWAITING fires only when every LWP is blocked; preempting a thread interrupts its system call, which must restart.
distractors: No end-to-end benchmarks; assumes interrupts rarely block.
Simulation only, with synthetic workloads.
Uniprocessor only, on a small-memory machine.

cards.question: Fedorova et al. (2004), "Chip Multithreading Systems Need a New Operating System Scheduler": what problem motivates the paper?
cards.answer: Server workloads leave a processor's pipeline as little as 19% utilized, and a naive scheduler on a chip-multithreading (CMT) processor can waste up to half its performance.
distractors: Kernel locks limit scalability on multiprocessors.
User-level threads waste kernel resources.
Event-driven web servers block on disk I/O.

cards.question: Fedorova et al.: why can't the OS scheduler just try every way of placing threads on hardware contexts and keep the best?
cards.answer: The number of combinations explodes (e.g., 100 threads on 16 contexts), so trying them all doesn't scale.
distractors: The hardware doesn't allow threads to move between contexts.
CPI can't be measured at all.
There are only a few combinations, so there's nothing to search.

cards.question: Processor design (Fedorova et al.): what is CMP, chip multiprocessing?
cards.answer: Multiple cores on one chip.
distractors: One core with several hardware contexts.
Multiple multithreaded cores on one chip.
One core issuing instructions from several threads in the same cycle.

cards.question: Processor design (Fedorova et al.): what is hardware multithreading (MT) on a single core?
cards.answer: One core with several hardware contexts (register sets) whose threads share the core's pipeline.
distractors: Multiple cores on one chip.
Multiple multithreaded cores on one chip.
A user-level threads library.
